text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure: each token kept privately gives me +1 but costs the other three members 0.75 each, while tokens put into the group account give me only +0.75 back. I'm setting up the math to compare total points under different contribution scenarios.

Since 1 > 0.75 for me individually regardless of what others do, keeping tokens private is the dominant strategy, even though full contribution would maximize the group's total welfare. This is a classic public goods dilemma — the Nash equilibrium has everyone hoarding their 20 tokens, each ending up with 65 points, which is worse than if everyone had cooperated.

Since this is a repeated 10-round game, reciprocity could sustain cooperation over time. For my opening move, I'll contribute the full 20 to the group as a cooperative signal and see how others respond before adjusting.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure of this token game: keeping a token gives me 1 point but costs each other player 0.75, while contributing to the group account gives me 0.75 with no cost to others. I'm setting up the equation for my total payoff based on how many tokens I keep versus how many everyone contributes to the group.

Comparing the marginal returns, keeping yields 1 point versus 0.75 for the group, so the dominant strategy is to keep all tokens individually—even though the group collectively does better if everyone contributes, since 0.75 points per token distributed across 4 people outweighs the 1 point from keeping. This is a classic social dilemma: individually rational to defect, but collectively better to cooperate.

Given this is a repeated 10-round game, I can try establishing cooperation through signaling, similar to tit-for-tat. For round 1, I'll contribute my full 20 tokens to the group account to signal cooperative intent and see how others respond.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game where each token I keep privately earns me 1 point but costs others 0.75 each, while tokens I put in the group account earn everyone 0.75. I'm working out that the privately optimal strategy for me is to keep everything, while the socially optimal outcome is for everyone to contribute fully to the group.

So the dominant strategy is clear: keeping tokens privately always beats contributing, yielding a Nash equilibrium where everyone contributes nothing, versus the cooperative optimum of full contribution yielding 60 each. Since this is a 10-round repeated game with unknown opponents, I'm weighing whether to open generously to signal cooperation, but running the numbers shows that if I contribute fully while others defect, I end up worse off than just defecting myself.

Given the small individual cost of cooperating early (about 5 points if others keep everything), I'll go with contributing 20 to the group pot in round 1 as a cooperation signal.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game where each member gets 20 tokens, and I'm working out the payoff structure: keeping a token privately gives me 1 point but costs each other member 0.75, while contributing to the group gives me 0.75 and costs others nothing. I'm trying to figure out my total points based on how many tokens I keep versus what others keep.

Socially, total points across all members are maximized when everyone contributes everything to the group, yielding 60 points each versus only 45 each if everyone keeps everything privately. But individually, keeping a token always nets me a slight advantage (1 vs 0.75) even though it costs the group more overall — this is the classic social dilemma where individual rationality (keep everything, dominant strategy) conflicts with collective welfare (contribute everything).

Since this is a 10-round repeated game, there's room to build trust across rounds. For round 1, I'll open with full cooperation and contribute all 20 tokens to the group, accepting the risk of exploitation in favor of signaling trustworthiness and aiming for the socially optimal outcome.

Since the group has sustained cooperation throughout, defecting now purely for a small personal gain would be selfish and undermine that trust even though there's no future round to protect. I'll stick with contributing the full 20 to honor the cooperative norm we've built.
